short: Influence of processing route on microstructure and wear res
title: Influence of processing route on microstructure and wear resistance of fly ash reinforced AZ31 magnesium matrix composites

lanes.label: Classical tools
lanes.sub: collapsed to one node per state

states.title: Hypothesis and design
states.head: Magnesium alloys are too soft for sliding-contact parts; a cheap reinforcement is needed that actually raises wear resistance. The processing route, not the reinforcement itself, decides the dispersion, the interface and the grain size of a fly-ash/AZ31 composite, and hence its wear behaviour.
states.detail: Absorbed: d1 (HYP/need), d2 (HYP/hypothesis), d3 (DES/base_system), d4 (DES/modification), d5 (DES/variable_sweep), d6 (PRC/forming), d7 (PRC/treatment), d8 (PRC/stimulus). Premises: Fly ash is a waste-derived powder of mainly SiO2 and Al2O3 whose density is close to that of molten magnesium, so it stays suspended; FSP is a hot-working route that refines grains by dynamic recrystallisation and disperses particles by three-dimensional material flow

states.title: Structure state
states.head: Stir casting leaves the fly ash bunched, with fields full of particles and fields with none; FSP scatters it through every section of the stir zone. The cast particles sit in haloes of reaction debris from contact with the 720 C melt; the FSP particles have sharp, debris-free boundaries with the matrix.

states.title: Property state and mechanisms
states.head: Microhardness is 94 HV after FSP against 62 HV as cast, a 51% gain. The FSP composite wears about 33% more slowly (280 against 420 x10-5 mm3/m) and with a lower friction coefficient.
states.detail: Absorbed: d13 (PRP/value), d14 (PRP/value), d15 (PRP/behavior_class), d16 (MEC/pathway), d18 (MEC/pathway). Premises: Archard's wear law: wear rate varies inversely with hardness; Parallel grooves on a worn surface indicate abrasive wear; smeared and transferred layers indicate the adhesive wear typical of unreinforced magnesium; Hall-Petch hardening with grain refinement and Orowan strengthening by fine dispersed particles

states.title: Performance state
states.head: Under 20 N dry sliding the FSP composite loses about 240 um of height against 350 um for the casting, with a steady rather than a spiky wear record

states.title: Conclusion
states.head: The route decides the composite: FSP gives homogeneous dispersion, clean interfaces and 4 um grains, and with them higher hardness and a third less wear

use: Fig. 6(c) and (d) show nanometric level debris dispersed in the matrix and in the vicinity of the large disintegrated particles.
The stir cast MMC shows a coarser grain structure (Fig. 7(a)) with an average grain size of $1 4 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ (Table 3).
On the contrary, fine and equiaxed grains with an average grain size (Table 3) of $4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ can be seen (Fig. 7(b)) in the MMC using FSP method.
However, larger crater due to the plowing action and piling of deformed material at the ridges of the grooves are observed on the worn surface of the stir cast composite (Fig. 10(a)).
On the contrary, the worn surface of FSP composite is covered by numerous fine debris (Fig. 10(b)).
This process produces larger size wear debris (Fig. 11(a)) which indicates bulk removal of the material causing higher wear rate.
The fine debris (Fig. 11(b)) trapped on the sliding track and at the sliding interface provide a rolling action and are accountable to initiate three body abrasion.
